evaluation.positioning_hook: A grieving miniaturist’s family unravels after her daughter’s death, as the house itself becomes a trap for a hereditary possession that turns guilt into ritual.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is immediately legible and highly sellable: a family grief story that detonates into supernatural horror, with a clear emotional spine and a memorable visual identity. The funeral, the support group, the miniature art, and the possession escalation give it broad genre appeal with strong word-of-mouth potential.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early and cleanly: a mother who builds miniatures is forced to confront a death in the family that may be tied to a demonic inheritance. The script keeps the engine clear through Annie’s workshop, Charlie’s behavior, the seance material, and the final reveal.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Annie is a loaded lead role built on grief, control, artistry, and denial, and Peter’s collapse gives the story a second emotional center. Steve and Charlie are also sharply usable, with the family dynamic generating strong scene-to-scene tension.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The miniature motif is not decorative; it becomes the script’s governing language, from Annie’s art to the house-as-diorama reveal to the final image. The story commits hard to a tragic, occult-family nightmare and keeps finding new ways to make the domestic space feel authored by something larger.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script escalates with real force: funeral unease, family fracture, seance discovery, possession events, attic reveal, and then a relentless final movement into the treehouse ritual. Each turn adds pressure and the ending lands with the kind of inevitability that makes the whole piece feel engineered.

resonant_originality.reasoning: It feels fresh because the supernatural mechanics are fused to a very specific family psychology and a very specific visual system. The miniature house, the inherited symbols, and the possession lineage create a premise that feels both strange and instantly coherent.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world is rich with tactile detail: the workshop, the school, the support group, the occult books, the attic, the treehouse, and the ritual objects all feel story-bearing. The script also gives the family home a lived-in institutional and emotional history that deepens the horror.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unmistakable: domestic realism, grief comedy, and occult dread are braided together without losing control of the register. The script can move from awkward family dinner to body-horror possession to ritual apocalypse and still feel of one piece.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the horror engine is a deeper story about maternal ambivalence, inherited trauma, and the terror of family identity. The support group, the sleepwalking history, and the mother-daughter lineage all suggest a much larger emotional architecture than the plot initially advertises.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The family triangle between Annie, Steve, and Peter is combustible, and Charlie adds a distinct, eerie counterpoint that keeps every interaction charged. Joan and the school/community figures widen the web enough that the relationships keep generating new pressure.

casting_characteristics: Teen and child roles for Peter and Charlie
Strong adult lead roles for Annie and Steve
One principal supporting role for Joan

notable_requirements: Family house with attic, workshop, treehouse, and bedroom spaces
Funeral home chapel and viewing room
High school classroom, gym, hallway, and party house

technical.vfx_details: Practical and digital augmentation for possession effects, floating body moments, fire transitions, and the final ritual imagery; miniature inserts and match-cut scale work are central to the design.
technical.sfx_needs: Fire effects, prosthetic decapitation imagery, flies/ants, practical blood and body-state effects, and controlled environmental effects for doors, lights, and movement.

rights_flags.detail: Serafem and Lexapro are named in Steve’s psychiatry scenes.
Facebook is referenced in Peter’s school and party material.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: premium theatrical horror / elevated streamer horror
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with strong festival-to-platform or specialty theatrical runway

cost.note: The footprint is mostly contained to a family house and a handful of practical locations, but the possession effects, fire work, and final ritual sequence push above micro-budget.

cast.note: The film depends on four strong central performances, including two younger roles, plus a memorable supporting turn for Joan.

location.note: The story stays largely contained, but it still moves through the house, school, support group, party house, apartment, cemetery, and attic/treehouse spaces.

content.note: The script includes decapitation, body horror, child endangerment, possession imagery, suicide references, and intense psychological distress.

rights.note: The script uses a small number of named brands and no major IP or real-person dependency.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The miniature motif is the movie’s engine.
strengths.what_it_means: That visual system gives the film a signature that buyers can market in one image and that directors can build an entire language around. Horror fans and prestige genre buyers alike will chase a film that turns the house, the art, and the family into the same object.
strengths.evidence: Annie’s workshop, the dollhouse-style Graham house, and the final image of the house as a miniature replica.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Annie is a showcase lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The part gives an actress grief, rage, denial, dark humor, and full-body terror in one arc, which is exactly the kind of role that can anchor a festival breakout or prestige horror campaign. Mid-career dramatic leads and actors looking for a career-reframing genre turn will line up for this.
strengths.evidence: The funeral eulogy, the support group confession, the workshop breakdown, and the final possession sequence.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The family drama is brutally playable.
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives producers a three-hander core that can carry the movie even before the supernatural machinery fully reveals itself. Actors who want emotionally combustible material — especially prestige drama leads and strong younger performers — will see immediate value here.
strengths.evidence: The dinner-table blowup, the bedroom confrontations, and the aftermath scenes between Annie, Steve, and Peter.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The horror escalates from grief, not gimmick.
strengths.what_it_means: That makes the scares feel earned and gives the movie a deeper emotional aftertaste than a standard possession title. Buyers looking for elevated genre with a human hook will recognize the difference immediately.
strengths.evidence: The support group, the sleepwalking history, Joan’s seance, and the final revelation of the ritual lineage.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The final act is a full-throttle reveal.
strengths.what_it_means: The ending pays off the film’s symbols, family history, and occult breadcrumbs in a way that feels designed for audience shock and post-screening conversation. That kind of climax is exactly what gives a horror title legs in theatrical and streaming conversation.
strengths.evidence: The attic discovery, the ritual books, the treehouse ceremony, and the final coronation of Peter.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The house feels like a haunted system.
strengths.what_it_means: The setting is not just a backdrop; it behaves like a machine that stores memory, guilt, and ritual, which gives the production a strong central arena. Directors and designers who love controlled, story-generating spaces will be drawn to that kind of architecture.
strengths.evidence: The workshop, attic, bedrooms, hallway, and the recurring miniature-house compositions.

whats_special.headline: This is elevated horror with a real prestige spine: a mother, son, and father trapped inside a family history that turns grief into ritual and the home into a diorama of doom. The script has a rare combination of commercial clarity, visual identity, and actor bait — the kind of package that can travel from genre buyers to prestige-minded producers without changing a word.

lead_characters.name: Annie Graham
lead_characters.hook: Annie is a grief-struck miniaturist whose need to control form is the perfect mask for a life coming apart at the seams. She’s brittle, funny, defensive, and deeply wounded, with a mind that keeps trying to impose order on experiences that refuse to stay contained.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Toni Collette in Hereditary itself and of Olivia Colman in The Lost Daughter — a woman whose interior collapse is played with precision, volatility, and dark wit. It gives an actress the rare chance to move from domestic realism to possession horror without ever losing emotional truth, which is catnip for prestige leads and awards-minded genre performers.

lead_characters.name: Steve Graham
lead_characters.hook: Steve is the family’s self-appointed stabilizer: controlled, rational, and increasingly cornered by events that his professional language can’t contain. He’s the kind of man who believes composure is love, until composure becomes its own form of denial.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Keaton in Birdman or Mark Ruffalo in Spotlight — a man trying to keep the room from collapsing while his own authority erodes in real time. Actors who specialize in contained intensity and late-breaking emotional rupture will want this because it lets them play restraint as a pressure cooker.

lead_characters.name: Peter Graham
lead_characters.hook: Peter is a socially awkward, emotionally flooded teenager who looks like he’s already halfway out of his own body. He’s horny, embarrassed, frightened, and guilt-ridden, which makes him the perfect vessel for a story about inheritance and possession.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea — a young man carrying grief, shame, and panic in a way that feels physically lived-in. It gives a young actor a rare chance to play a passive-seeming character whose internal collapse becomes the movie’s final engine.

lead_characters.name: Charlie Graham
lead_characters.hook: Charlie is an eerie, self-contained kid whose silence, tics, and outsider energy make her feel like she’s receiving the world on a different frequency. She’s not a conventional child character; she’s a presence, a mystery, and eventually a tragic pivot point.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Brooklynn Prince in The Florida Project — a child performance that can be strange, funny, and devastating without ever feeling manufactured. It gives a young actor a role with iconic imagery, behavioral specificity, and the kind of haunting screen memory that can define a career early.

lead_characters.name: Joan
lead_characters.hook: Joan arrives as a warm, grieving older woman and gradually reveals herself as the story’s most unnerving human hinge. She’s maternal, persuasive, and spiritually committed in a way that feels both comforting and dangerous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Ann Dowd in The Handmaid’s Tale — a character who can pivot from tenderness to menace without changing her temperature. Character actors who specialize in authority, ambiguity, and moral unease will chase this because the role can dominate every scene she enters.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Mason
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Mason is the professional face of reason who walks into a house already ruled by forces he can’t diagnose. He’s calm, polished, and briefly useful, which makes his eventual helplessness land harder.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Richard Jenkins in The Visitor — a grounded, humane professional whose competence is tested by something larger than his vocabulary. A seasoned character actor can make this role memorable by playing the exact point where expertise stops helping.

lead_characters.name: Bridget
lead_characters.hook: Bridget is the cool, slightly detached classmate who becomes Peter’s first real adolescent fixation. She’s not overbuilt, but she gives the teen world a pulse and a social reality outside the family house.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Kaitlyn Dever in Booksmart — a sharp, low-key teen role that can register instantly with very little screen time. Young actors who know how to make a few looks and lines feel lived-in will want it because it gives the movie a believable outside world.

lead_characters.name: Mr. Davies
lead_characters.hook: Mr. Davies is the classroom adult who keeps trying to turn tragedy into discussion, only to watch Peter drift further away from the room. He’s a functional authority figure with just enough personality to make the school scenes feel specific.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of the teacher roles in Lady Bird or Eighth Grade — a small part that can become memorable through timing and specificity. Working character actors will like it because it gives them a clean, grounded lane inside a high-intensity movie.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make horror feel authored, intimate, and emotionally devastating.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie directors with at least one or two features, plus genre filmmakers who already care about performance and visual grammar more than body count. This material rewards directors who like controlled compositions, domestic spaces that become psychological traps, and escalation that feels inevitable rather than noisy.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a rare chance to build dread through blocking, production design, and family performance instead of constant external action. It’s especially attractive to filmmakers who can turn a contained house, a few key locations, and a strong visual motif into a signature calling card.

buyer_appeal.detail: The Annie role can anchor the package with one major performance, while the contained house-centered structure keeps the spend in a controllable lane. The occult-family premise, strong poster image, and final-act shock give it the kind of theatrical-to-streaming afterlife buyers want from elevated horror.

considerations.area: The family triangle carries the whole engine.
considerations.detail: The script already has a strong central pressure point, but the version that keeps Annie, Steve, and Peter’s emotional collisions as the primary driver will preserve the movie’s power even when the supernatural material is stripped away. One lever would be to keep every major reveal tethered to a family choice or accusation, so the horror always lands as an extension of the relationship drama.

considerations.area: The occult reveal arrives in a long tail.
considerations.detail: The final mythology payoff is satisfying, but it comes after a substantial run of grief, suspicion, and domestic fracture. A next pass could consider how early the audience needs the first clean breadcrumb of the ritual system so the back half can feel even more inevitable without losing mystery.

considerations.area: The supporting world is efficient, not expansive.
considerations.detail: The script is strongest when it stays inside the house and the immediate orbit around it, which is also what keeps the production footprint attractive. If a producer wanted to simplify further, the version that folds a couple of school or community beats into fewer locations would protect the momentum without changing the story’s core.

considerations.area: The possession imagery is the main technical spend.
considerations.detail: The fire transitions, floating-body moments, ants, flies, and final ritual tableau are the places where the effects plan has to be precise. A practical-heavy approach with selective digital support would protect the grounded feel and keep the movie in the right budget lane.

considerations.area: Charlie’s presence is the emotional fuse.
considerations.detail: The script uses Charlie as both a character and a haunting image, which is one of its sharpest choices. A future pass could keep foregrounding the specific behaviors that make her feel singular — the clicking, the drawings, the treehouse, the shoebox — because those details are doing a lot of the movie’s atmospheric work.
